title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson about the security review for a client engagement, what is the central focus?
options: Practicing security from the first scoping call with a threat model, secrets hygiene, and compliance evidence instead of a final gate
A history of security standards
A review of unrelated scanning tools
A summary of procurement policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that security is a constraint you design against from the start, not a downstream gate to clear at the end.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Name only the external attacker as the actor in the threat model
A threat model names the assets, the actors including the insider and prompt injection, and the trust boundaries the actors must cross
Write the threat model at the end once the answers are settled
A profile is itself a security boundary that sandboxes the agent
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the threats that break agent deployments are usually the insider and the prompt injection, not the hacker in the parking lot.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Answer compliance with assurances that the system is fine
Secrets can live in a prompt as long as they are needed for the task
Least privilege gives each agent the narrowest set of credentials the task requires, and compliance is answered with evidence, not claims
One approval mode can be a blanket across interactive and unattended work
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that secrets are scoped to the narrowest task and compliance is satisfied by legible records and documentation, not assurances.

questions.question: Per the lesson about working with IT, compliance, and legal, what is the central focus?
options: A history of corporate governance
A review of unrelated legal tools
Treating a rollout as a stakeholder channel, triaging the three teams in early, and planning it backward from the go-live date
A summary of sales policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the rollout lives in other people's workflows and is a stakeholder channel to plan, not a hurdle to clear at the end.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: IT, compliance, and legal are a single obstacle to plan against as one
Build the agent first and ask how long the rollout will take after
Present the same demonstration deck to every team
Start the sticky gates, legal review, procurement, IT provisioning, in parallel with the build so the channel is open when the agent is ready
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches backward planning: the slowest gate is the schedule, so sticky gates start in week one while the build runs.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Compliance wants a feature demo and IT wants your enthusiasm
To IT present the agent as a component that must operate safely, to compliance as a demonstrable process, and to legal as contractually bounded scope
Write the statement of work about the agent you are building, not the deliverable
A rollout ends at go-live the day the agent starts
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the same decision is translated into each team's language, and each team gets the artifact it acts on.

questions.question: Per the lesson about pricing engagements, what is the central focus?
options: Choosing between fixed-fee and time-and-materials by allocating estimation risk, priced from a real unit economy and defended with change control
A history of consulting fees
A review of unrelated billing tools
A summary of accounting policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the price is a risk allocation you choose, not a number you pick, and the contract mechanism decides who carries the uncertainty.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Fixed-fee is the right call when you do not know the work, because it gives the client certainty
Time-and-materials is the right call when the scope is understood and the environment is known
Fixed-fee is right when you genuinely know the work, and T&M is honest when you cannot name the deliverable
The client should always hold the estimation risk because they have deeper pockets
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that fixed-fee is for known work and T&M for exploratory work, with the risk sitting on the side that can best manage it.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Change control is a scope skill separate from pricing
A fixed-fee with no enforced change control quietly becomes time-and-materials where you forgot to charge the time
Every addition to a fixed-fee engagement is absorbed into the margin to keep the client happy
A T&M engagement needs no budget guardrail because the client chose it
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the price is only as stable as the change control that defends it, so a fixed-fee must enforce its boundary.

questions.question: Per the lesson about writing proposals and statements of work, what is the central focus?
options: A history of contract law
A review of unrelated document tools
A summary of accounting policy
Writing the proposal and SOW as risk documents with a specific scope boundary, testable acceptance criteria, and written exclusions and change control
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the only protection that works in a dispute is specificity, and templates are specifically vague.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A scope that says deliver an agent that improves the support workflow is a strong boundary
An acceptance criterion is a test, not a description, so the agent clears ninety percent of the golden set is better than it should be accurate
Name only what you will do, and leave the out-of-scope list out
Keep the price assumptions silent so you are not pinned down
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that an acceptance criterion is a test you can run and count, and an out-of-scope list is a fence that protects the fixed-fee.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Change control is an adversarial device to protect only you
Nothing material needs to appear in both the proposal and the SOW
A payment schedule that does not match the pricing risk allocation is a second conflicting contract that will win
Leave the price assumptions out of the SOW to stay flexible
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the payment terms must match the risk allocation you chose, because a mismatch becomes a second contract that wins the argument.

questions.question: Per the lesson about managing scope creep and difficult clients, what is the central focus?
options: Settling scope creep and difficult clients with a written scope, a named acceptance bar, and a change process
A review of negotiation tactics
A history of client management
A summary of HR policy
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that creep and difficult clients are one problem, the engagement drifting from its baseline, fixed by three structural artifacts.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Scope creep is a failure of will, so the fix is learning to say no
A baseline nobody signed is still a boundary you can hold
Run the change-order process on every request past the baseline, including ones you would do for free, so every change is visible
Gold-plating is good diligence that builds client trust
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that every change carries a visible trade, which makes the client selective and prevents silent erosion of the fee.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: When a client disputes the evidence, defend your work with words and your expertise
The ghost who goes silent needs a dated gate that can fail, and the arguer needs an artifact to confront
A reviewer who is never accountable will eventually respond on their own
Fight every escalation at the requester lane even when the scope keeps moving
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that each difficult-client pattern has a named move: a gate that can fail for the ghost and an artifact for the arguer.
